title: Airbnb check-in instructions and self check-in: templates for every kind of door
summary: Copyable Airbnb check-in instructions for keypads, lockboxes, buzzers and late arrivals, plus a self check-in checklist and a lockout plan.
body_markdown:
[All posts](https://prohost.ai/blog)


**Check-in is the one moment of a stay when the guest can't wait for you. They're standing at the door after a long drive, often at dusk, often with a tired kid or a dead phone battery, and the only thing between them and a good first impression is a message you wrote weeks ago. Most of the 4 p.m. "how do I get in" texts hosts get are not about a broken lock. They're about instructions that were sent too early, buried in a paragraph, or missing the one detail that matters at that particular door. Here are the check-in messages we'd send for each kind of entry, the self check-in setup behind them, and the plan for when it still goes wrong.**


## Key takeaways


- **Most stays start at 3 or 4 p.m.** Across about 404,000 recent stays on ProhostAI, 48.8% checked in at 16:00 and 38.0% at 15:00. Your message has to work for a guest arriving in that window and for the one who lands at midnight.
- **Hosts send check-in messages at very different times.** The median goes out 24 hours before arrival, but a quarter go out in the last 3 hours and a quarter 48 hours or more ahead. The day before is the sweet spot: close enough to be read, early enough to ask questions.
- **Every line should be a step.** Address, time, parking, the door, Wi-Fi. Anything else belongs in the guidebook.
- **Give each stay its own code, with the time it starts working.** Airbnb's own hosting guidance says to give each booking guest a unique access code.
- **Have a lockout plan before you need one.** A backup way in, a phone that gets answered, and a rule for who drives over.

## Where we're coming from


We host in Hawaii, the Smokies and Joshua Tree, and hold a[4.99 rating across thousands of guest stays](https://prohost.ai/about) . Before ProhostAI I spent 6 years at Airbnb as a staff data scientist on the hosting team. ProhostAI has sent more than 750,000 guest messages across 13,000+ properties.


In that data, check-in times cluster hard (16:00, then 15:00, then 14:00 for about 5% of stays) while the timing of the check-in message doesn't cluster at all.


*How we measured: check-in times are from about 404,000 confirmed stays that checked out in the last 12 months, in each listing's local time. Message timing is from 22,191 check-in messages sent by 85 workspaces in the 7 days before arrival over the same period. Internal workspaces excluded (read-only aggregate of ProhostAI data, November 2026).*


## What Airbnb does for you, and what it doesn't


Airbnb has a built-in place for check-in details. In the Listing editor, open **Arrival guide** , choose a **Check-in method** (smart lock, keypad, lockbox, building staff, in-person greeting, or other) and write your instructions ([Airbnb Help, "How do I add check-in instructions to my listing?"](https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/1926) , checked 19 November 2026). Guests see the method right away. The detailed instructions stay hidden until 48 hours before check-in, and Airbnb sends a reservation reminder email with them. Airbnb's[self check-in guide for hosts](https://www.airbnb.com/resources/hosting-homes/a/how-to-provide-self-check-in-for-smooth-arrivals-238) adds that you can attach photos, and that "it's important to give each booking guest a unique access code."


Fill in the Arrival guide: it's the fallback a guest finds in the app. But it's written once per listing, so it can't carry a per-stay code, and it reaches Airbnb guests only. Treat the two as a pair. The Arrival guide holds what never changes: where the door is, how the lock works, where to park. Your own check-in message, sent the day before, holds what changes per stay (the code and the time it starts working) and repeats the three things a guest needs at the door.


## The check-in message templates


Each template is for the evening before arrival, around 6 p.m. local time. Keep the bold labels: guests scan for one word on a phone.


### 1. Keypad or smart lock


> Hi \[guest first name\], tomorrow's the day. Here's everything for arriving at \[listing name\]:
>
>
> **Address:** \[address\] (\[map link\])
> **Check-in:** from \[check-in time\]
> **Parking:** \[parking instructions\]
> **Getting in:** the keypad is on the \[front/side\] door. Enter \[door code\] and press \[lock button\]. Your code works from \[check-in time\] on \[check-in date\] until \[check-out time\] on \[check-out date\].
> **Wi-Fi:** \[wifi name\], password \[wifi password\]
>
>
> The guidebook has the rest, from the thermostat to the coffee maker: \[guidebook link\]. If anything is unclear on the way, message me here.


The line that prevents the most messages is "your code works from \[check-in time\]". A guest who arrives early to a dead code assumes the lock is broken.


### 2. Lockbox


> Hi \[guest first name\], here's how to get into \[listing name\] tomorrow.
>
>
> **Address:** \[address\] (\[map link\])
> **Check-in:** from \[check-in time\]
> **Parking:** \[parking instructions\]
> **The key:** the lockbox is \[exact location, e.g. on the railing to the left of the front door\]. Enter \[lockbox code\], pull the shackle down, and take the key. Please put the lockbox back closed and scrambled.
> **Wi-Fi:** \[wifi name\], password \[wifi password\]
>
>
> When you leave, the key goes back in the same lockbox. Message me here with any questions.


Lockboxes fail when the guest can't find the box. Describe its location the way a stranger would, attach a photo in the Arrival guide, and change the code between stays if the box allows it.


### 3. In-person meet


> Hi \[guest first name\], looking forward to meeting you tomorrow at \[listing name\].
>
>
> **Address:** \[address\] (\[map link\])
> **Meeting time:** \[time\]. If your plans change, message me here and I'll adjust.
> **Parking:** \[parking instructions\]
> **Finding me:** I'll be \[where, e.g. at the front door\]. If I'm a minute late, my number is \[phone\].
>
>
> It takes about 10 minutes: I'll hand over the keys, show you the Wi-Fi and the heating, and leave you to settle in.


Ask for the arrival time in the welcome message and confirm it in this one.


### 4. Apartment building with a lobby or buzzer


> Hi \[guest first name\], here's the way in to \[listing name\], apartment \[unit number\], tomorrow.
>
>
> **Address:** \[street address\], \[building name\]
> **Check-in:** from \[check-in time\]
> **Building door:** \[buzzer instructions, e.g. press \[code\] on the panel\] or \[lobby instructions, e.g. the front desk has your name\]
> **Elevator / stairs:** \[floor\], turn \[left/right\]. The door is number \[unit number\].
> **Apartment door:** \[lock instructions and door code\]
> **Parking:** \[garage, street rules or the nearest paid lot\]
> **Wi-Fi:** \[wifi name\], password \[wifi password\]
>
>
> Please don't buzz or ask neighbours to let you in; the building is strict about it. Message me here if the front door gives you any trouble.


Two doors means two chances to get stuck. List the steps in the order the guest meets them.


### 5. Late-night arrival


Send this when a guest tells you they'll arrive after 9 p.m., on top of the standard message.


> Hi \[guest first name\], thanks for letting me know you'll arrive around \[time\]. Self check-in works any time after \[check-in time\], so there's no rush. A few things for a late arrival:
>
>
> **Lights:** \[porch light / motion light / where the switch is\]
> **Quiet:** the neighbours are asleep by then, so please keep car doors and voices down on the way in.
> **If you get stuck:** call \[phone\]. That line is answered at night.
>
>
> Drive safe, and see the guidebook for anything you need tonight: \[guidebook link\].


Only promise a line that gets answered at night if one does.


### 6. Reply to an early check-in request


The most common reply you'll send around check-in. Two versions, depending on the calendar.


> **When the calendar allows it:** Good news, \[guest first name\]: nobody checks out of \[listing name\] the night before, so we can have it ready for you at \[early time\]. Early check-in is \[price or free\]. \[If paid: Here's the link to add it: \[link\].\] I'll update your door code to work from \[early time\].


> **When it doesn't:** I'd love to, \[guest first name\], but another guest checks out that morning and our cleaners need the time in between. Your door code will work from \[check-in time\]. If you arrive early, you're welcome to \[luggage option, if any\] and I'll message you here the moment the place is ready.


Check the calendar and the cleaning schedule before you say yes. A yes you take back costs more than a no.


## The self check-in setup checklist


The message is only as good as the setup behind it. Before you switch to self check-in, check each line:


1. **The lock works without you.** Fresh batteries, a tested code, and a lock that doesn't depend on the guest's phone having signal.
2. **One code per stay.** Each code starts at check-in time and ends at checkout. A code that never changes is a code that's been shared.
3. **A backup way in.** A second code, a lockbox with a spare key, or a neighbour who can help. The backup needs its own instructions, kept out of the guest message until it's needed.
4. **The Arrival guide is filled in** , with the method, a photo of the door and lock, and parking.
5. **The address finds the door** in two map apps. If a pin lands on the wrong side of the block, add a landmark.
6. **Outdoor light** at the door, on a timer or a motion sensor.
7. **The house rules guests need on arrival** are in the guidebook. Our[house rules template](https://prohost.ai/blog/airbnb-house-rules-template) covers the full set.
8. **Someone answers the phone** when guests arrive, including after 9 p.m.


## The lockout plan


Decide the steps before the first lockout:


1. **The guest calls or messages.** The answer has to come in minutes, not hours. A guest who can't reach you will try Airbnb next, and that is not where you want this conversation to go.
2. **Try the simple fixes first.** Is it after the start time? Did they press the lock button? Is the battery dead (many keypads show a light)? Is this the right door?
3. **Send the backup.** A second code, or the spare key location.
4. **Send a person** if the backup fails. Know who that is for each listing before it happens.
5. **Fix the cause the next day.** Replace the battery, rewrite the confusing line, add the photo.

## Keep it running


A check-in message you have to remember to send will eventually not be sent. In ProhostAI it's a[scheduled message](https://prohost.ai/features/scheduled-messages) : a check-in rule that sends at the offset you choose before arrival, with a version per listing where the doors differ. The placeholders fill in the guest's name, dates, address, Wi-Fi and the door code for that stay.


With a smart lock connected through[smart devices](https://prohost.ai/features/smart-devices) , every reservation gets its own code with start and end times, and the door-code placeholder drops that code into the message. When Autopilot confirms a late checkout, it writes the new time to the reservation and the code's window follows it.


The questions that follow ("can we check in at 1?") are for[Autopilot](https://prohost.ai/features/autopilot) and Gabby, the Guest Experience Manager AI employee. Gabby answers from the listing details and the guidebook, and offers early check-in when the calendar allows it; paid early check-in runs through[upsells](https://prohost.ai/features/upsells) . Complaints, refunds and anything about safety go straight to a person.


For the guest who calls instead of texting,[AI Phone](https://prohost.ai/ai-phone) answers with the same property knowledge, matches the caller to their reservation, and hands the call to you by the rules you set. What still needs a person: driving over, a physically broken lock, and a guest who is upset rather than confused.

## FAQ


**When should I send check-in instructions?** The evening before arrival, around 6 p.m. local time, and the morning of arrival for same-day bookings. Airbnb releases the Arrival guide details 48 hours before check-in, so your own message the day before is a reminder close to the moment the guest needs it.


**Should I put the door code in Airbnb's Arrival guide?** No. A code in the Arrival guide never changes, and yours should change with every stay. Put the method and the location of the lock in the Arrival guide, and send the per-stay code in your message.


**What's the most common Airbnb check-in time?** On ProhostAI, 16:00 for 48.8% of stays and 15:00 for 38.0%. If your cleaning regularly runs late, a 16:00 check-in buys you an hour.


**How do I handle a guest who arrives before check-in time?** Tell them in the check-in message exactly when the code starts working. If they ask, check the calendar first, then offer early check-in or a luggage option.


**Do I need a smart lock for self check-in?** No. A keypad or lockbox works. A smart lock lets you issue a unique code per stay automatically, which is the part that's hard to do by hand.


## The takeaway


Check-in instructions are a list of steps for a tired person at a door. Send them the day before. Lead with the address, time, parking, door and Wi-Fi, and say when the code starts working. Keep the fixed details in Airbnb's Arrival guide and the per-stay code in your message, and decide your lockout plan before you need it. The[other messages in a stay](https://prohost.ai/blog/airbnb-message-templates) , from the welcome to the review request, follow the same rule: short, timed, and written for a phone.
